Numbers Stations Frequency List

The A-26 EIBI schedule lists 11 numbers and mystery stations on 79 frequencies. Numbers stations don't publish schedules, so these entries come from hobbyist logs. Times are UTC and can change without notice. For what they are and who runs them, read Numbers Stations Explained.

Reading Numbers Station Names

Hobbyists identify numbers stations with the ENIGMA 2000 system: E for English voice, S for Slavic languages, V for other languages and M for Morse. Entries labelled as channel markers, buzzers or pips are mystery and utility transmitters rather than voice number readers.

Are numbers stations still on the air?

The A-26 EIBI schedule still lists 11 numbers and mystery stations on 79 frequencies, compiled from hobbyist logs. Individual stations can go silent, move or change times without notice, so treat the list as a guide.

What frequencies do numbers stations use?

They are spread across the shortwave bands. The frequencies with the most logged entries in the schedule are 3243, 3364, 3850, 4909, 4940 kHz.

How can I listen to numbers stations online?

Open a free WebSDR or KiwiSDR receiver in your browser and tune to a listed frequency at the listed UTC time. Our Listen Online page links to receivers and explains how to tune.

Do numbers stations publish a schedule?

No. Their operators do not publish schedules, so every time in this list comes from listener observations compiled in the EIBI database.
